statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a continuous surjection of [compact metric spaces](c:compact-metric-space) whose fibres are [acyclic](c:acyclic-fibre) in [Čech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) with coefficients in an abelian group $G$. Then $f^*\colon \check H^q(Y;G) \to \check H^q(X;G)$ is an isomorphism for every $q \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are [compact metric spaces](c:compact-metric-space).
The map $f\colon X \to Y$ is continuous and surjective.
Every fibre $f^{-1}(y)$ is [acyclic](c:acyclic-fibre): $\check H^0(f^{-1}(y);G) = G$ and $\check H^q(f^{-1}(y);G) = 0$ for $q > 0$.

conclusion: The induced map $f^*\colon \check H^q(Y;G) \to \check H^q(X;G)$ is an isomorphism in every degree $q \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Leray spectral sequence of a closed map
proofs.slogan: Pass to sheaf cohomology, compute the direct images on the fibres, and let the Leray spectral sequence collapse onto one row.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with constant coefficients $G$. The same spectral sequence gives the truncated version: acyclic fibres in degrees below $n$ give an isomorphism below $n$.

roles.why: Compact Hausdorff spaces make Čech and sheaf cohomology agree and make closed subsets taut.
Surjectivity makes every fibre nonempty; a continuous map of compact spaces is closed, which gives base change on stalks.
Acyclic fibres kill the higher direct images and make the zeroth one the constant sheaf.

steps.slogan: Replace Čech cohomology by sheaf cohomology with constant coefficients.
steps.detail: On a compact Hausdorff space, [Čech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) with coefficients in $G$ equals the [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) of the constant sheaf $G$. This holds for $X$, for $Y$ and for every closed subset, so it also holds for the fibres.

steps.slogan: Compute the stalks of the higher direct images on the fibres.
steps.detail: The map $f$ is a [closed map](c:closed-map) of compact Hausdorff spaces, so closed subsets are taut. Hence the stalk of $R^q f_* G_X$ at $y$ is $\check H^q(f^{-1}(y);G)$ (proper base change).

steps.slogan: Use the acyclic fibres to kill the higher direct images.
steps.detail: By hypothesis these stalks are $0$ for $q > 0$, so $R^q f_* G_X = 0$ for $q > 0$. For $q = 0$ the stalk is $G$, and the unit map $G_Y \to f_* G_X$ is an isomorphism on every stalk, so $f_* G_X = G_Y$.

steps.slogan: Let the Leray spectral sequence collapse onto the row $q = 0$.
steps.detail: The [Leray spectral sequence](c:leray-spectral-sequence) $E_2^{p,q} = H^p(Y; R^q f_* G_X) \Rightarrow H^{p+q}(X; G_X)$ has $E_2^{p,q} = 0$ for $q > 0$. Only one row survives, so every differential is zero and the edge map $H^p(Y; G_Y) \to H^p(X; G_X)$ is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Identify the edge map with $f^*$ and return to Čech cohomology.
steps.detail: The edge map is induced by the adjunction map $G_Y \to f_* G_X$, and it equals the pull-back $f^*$. By step 1, $f^*$ is an isomorphism on Čech cohomology in every degree.

concepts.c:compact-metric-space: Compactness and the Hausdorff property give tautness and base change on stalks.
concepts.c:acyclic-fibre: Acyclic fibres make the higher direct images vanish and the zeroth one constant.
concepts.c:cech-cohomology: The theorem is stated for Čech cohomology, which the proof identifies with sheaf cohomology.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: Sheaf cohomology carries the Leray spectral sequence that the proof needs.
concepts.c:closed-map: A closed map lets the stalk of a direct image be computed on the fibre.
concepts.c:leray-spectral-sequence: It relates the cohomology of $X$ to that of $Y$ with fibre coefficients.

source.note: The standard sheaf-theoretic proof through the Leray spectral sequence of a closed map, as in Bredon, Sheaf Theory (2nd ed., GTM 170, Springer 1997) and Spanier, Algebraic Topology (McGraw-Hill 1966, chapter 6). The theorem is due to Vietoris and Begle (E. G. Begle, Ann. of Math. 51 (1950), 534-543).

statement: In an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle) with altitude $h$, the distances from a point $P$ inside the triangle, or on its boundary, to the three sides add up to $h$.

hypotheses.text: The triangle $ABC$ is [equilateral](c:equilateral-triangle) with side $a > 0$ and altitude $h$.
The point $P$ lies inside the triangle or on its boundary.

conclusion: $d_a + d_b + d_c = h$, where $d_a, d_b, d_c$ are the distances from $P$ to the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$.

proofs.name: Area decomposition
proofs.slogan: Cut the triangle into three triangles at the point and compare their total area with the area of the whole triangle.
proofs.scope: A point inside the triangle; for a boundary point one distance is $0$ and the same computation holds with a triangle of area $0$.

roles.why: Equal sides give the three small triangles the same base $a$, so the common factor $a/2$ cancels.
A point in the triangle cuts it into three triangles with disjoint interiors.

steps.slogan: Join $P$ to the three vertices to cut the triangle into three triangles.
steps.detail: The segments $PA$, $PB$ and $PC$ cut $ABC$ into triangles $PBC$, $PCA$ and $PAB$ with disjoint interiors. Hence the [areas](c:area) add: $[PBC] + [PCA] + [PAB] = [ABC]$.

steps.slogan: Write each small area as half the base times the distance to the base.
steps.detail: Triangle $PBC$ has base $BC = a$ and height $d_a$, so $[PBC] = \tfrac12 a d_a$. In the same way $[PCA] = \tfrac12 a d_b$ and $[PAB] = \tfrac12 a d_c$.

steps.slogan: Write the area of the whole triangle as half the side times the altitude.
steps.detail: The altitude $h$ is the distance from $A$ to the line $BC$, and $BC = a$, so $[ABC] = \tfrac12 a h$.

steps.slogan: Divide the area identity by $a/2$ to get the sum of the distances.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 give $\tfrac12 a (d_a + d_b + d_c) = \tfrac12 a h$. Since $a > 0$, it follows that $d_a + d_b + d_c = h$.

concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: Equal sides give one common base $a$ for all the area formulas.
concepts.c:area: The proof counts the area of the triangle in two ways.

source.note: The classical area proof of Viviani's theorem.

statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) and $X$ a finite ground set. Write $\mathcal A_x = \{A \in \mathcal A : x \in A\}$. If $\{\mathcal A_x : x \in X\}$ [shatters](c:shattering) a subfamily $S$ with $|S| \ge 2^n$, then $\mathcal A$ shatters some $n$-element set $T \subseteq X$.

hypotheses.text: The family $\mathcal A$ is a finite [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) and $X$ is a finite set of points.
The dual family $\{\mathcal A_x : x \in X\}$ [shatters](c:shattering) $S$: every subfamily $R \subseteq S$ equals $S \cap \mathcal A_x$ for some $x \in X$.
The subfamily $S$ has at least $2^n$ members.

conclusion: Some $T \subseteq X$ with $|T| = n$ is shattered by $\mathcal A$: every subset of $T$ equals $T \cap A$ for some $A \in \mathcal A$.

formal.difference: The declaration works for finite families over a type with decidable equality, which is a formal convenience only. It states the same combinatorial fact.

proofs.name: Bitstring coding
proofs.slogan: Embed the $n$-bit strings into $S$, read one ground point off each bit position, and check that these points are shattered.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $n = 0$: then $T = \emptyset$ works because $S \subseteq \mathcal A$ is nonempty.

roles.why: It supplies the members $A_b$ and the points $x_k$ that the construction uses.
Shattering gives, for each bit position, a point of $X$ that separates the strings with that bit set.
Having $2^n$ members lets an injection from the bit strings into $S$ exist.

steps.slogan: Show that the shattered subfamily $S$ lies inside $\mathcal A$.
steps.detail: Shattering the whole of $S$ gives some $x \in X$ with $S \cap \mathcal A_x = S$. Hence $S \subseteq \mathcal A_x \subseteq \mathcal A$.

steps.slogan: Embed the $2^n$ bit strings of length $n$ into $S$ by an injection.
steps.detail: Since $|S| \ge 2^n$, there is an injective map $b \mapsto A_b$ from $\{0,1\}^n$ into $S$.

steps.slogan: For each bit position $k$, pick a point $x_k$ that separates the strings with bit $k$ set.
steps.detail: Let $R_k = \{A_b : b_k = 1\} \subseteq S$. By [shattering](c:shattering) there is $x_k \in X$ with $S \cap \mathcal A_{x_k} = R_k$, so $x_k \in A_b$ if and only if $b_k = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the $n$ chosen points are pairwise distinct.
steps.detail:
For $j 
e k$, let $e_j$ be the string with a single $1$ at place $j$. Then $x_j \in A_{e_j}$ and $x_k 
otin A_{e_j}$, so $x_j 
e x_k$. Hence $T = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \subseteq X$ has $n$ points.

steps.slogan: Choose, for each subset of $T$, the member of $\mathcal A$ that cuts it out.
steps.detail: Let $t \subseteq T$ and put $b_k = 1$ exactly when $x_k \in t$. Then $A_b \in S \subseteq \mathcal A$ and $T \cap A_b = \{x_k : b_k = 1\} = t$. So $\mathcal A$ [shatters](c:shattering) $T$.

concepts.c:family-of-sets: The members $A_b$ of the family carry the bit patterns.
concepts.c:shattering: Shattering of $S$ is the hypothesis, and shattering of $T$ is the conclusion.

source.note: mathlib embeds the cube into S (cubeEmbedding), takes one column per bit through mem_dualFamily and the shattering hypothesis, proves the columns injective on singleton bitstrings, and returns the image of this injection.

statement: Nine abelian groups form a braid diagram with four strands: $E\to A\to B\to G\to K$, $E\to I\to J\to G\to C\to D$, $A\to F\to J\to K\to H\to D$ and $I\to F\to B\to C\to H$. If the diagram [commutes](c:commutative-diagram), strands 1 to 3 are [exact](c:exact-sequence) and strand 4 is a complex, then strand 4 is exact.

hypotheses.text: The braid diagram [commutes](c:commutative-diagram): $A \to B$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $I \to J$ and $J \to K$ each equal the composite through the middle group below or above them, and the three diamonds on $E,A,F,I$, on $F,B,G,J$ and on $G,C,H,K$ commute.
The strands 1, 2 and 3 are [exact sequences](c:exact-sequence) at each of their inner groups.
In strand 4, any two consecutive maps compose to zero.

conclusion: Strand 4, $I \to F \to B \to C \to H$, is exact at $F$, at $B$ and at $C$.

proofs.name: Diagram chase
proofs.slogan: Take a kernel element of strand 4 and chase it around the braid, one inner group at a time.
proofs.scope: Exactness at $F$, at $B$ and at $C$ is proved in three separate chases. The notation $XY$ stands for the map $X \to Y$.

roles.why: Commuting triangles and diamonds move an element from one strand to the next.
Exactness of strands 1 to 3 turns each vanishing image into a preimage.
A complex gives the easy inclusion of image in kernel and kills a correction term.

steps.slogan: Prove exactness of strand 4 at $F$ by chasing a kernel element of $FB$.
steps.detail: Let $x \in F$ with $FB(x) = 0$. The diamond on $F,B,G,J$ gives $JG(FJ(x)) = 0$, so strand 2 at $J$ gives $FJ(x) = IJ(i) = FJ(IF(i))$. Then $x' = x - IF(i)$ has $FJ(x') = 0 = FB(x')$, so strand 3 gives $x' = AF(a)$, and $AB(a) = FB(x') = 0$ gives $a = EA(e)$ by strand 1. The diamond on $E,A,F,I$ gives $x' = IF(EI(e))$, so $x \in \operatorname{im} IF$.

steps.slogan: Prove exactness of strand 4 at $B$ by chasing a kernel element of $BC$.
steps.detail: Let $x \in B$ with $BC(x) = 0$. Then $GC(BG(x)) = 0$, so strand 2 at $G$ gives $BG(x) = JG(j)$. Since $JK(j) = GK(BG(x)) = 0$, strand 3 at $J$ gives $j = FJ(f)$. The diamond gives $BG(x - FB(f)) = 0$, so strand 1 at $B$ gives $x - FB(f) = AB(a) = FB(AF(a))$, and $x \in \operatorname{im} FB$.

steps.slogan: Prove exactness of strand 4 at $C$ by chasing a kernel element of $CH$.
steps.detail: Let $x \in C$ with $CH(x) = 0$. Then $CD(x) = 0$, so strand 2 at $C$ gives $x = GC(g)$. The diamond on $G,C,H,K$ gives $KH(GK(g)) = 0$, so strand 3 at $K$ gives $GK(g) = JK(j) = GK(JG(j))$. Strand 1 at $G$ gives $g - JG(j) = BG(b)$, and $GC \circ JG = 0$, so $x = GC(BG(b)) = BC(b)$.

steps.slogan: Join the three chases to get exactness of strand 4.
steps.detail: Strand 4 is a complex, so image lies in kernel at $F$, $B$ and $C$. Steps 1 to 3 give kernel in image at the same three groups. So strand 4 is exact.

concepts.c:commutative-diagram: Commutation of triangles and diamonds lets the chase pass between strands.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness of three strands is what each chase uses.

source.note: The statement is that of the nLab page braid lemma, which credits Munkres, Elements of Algebraic Topology, section 26 (exercise). The chase is written out here.

statement: Taking normalized chains is an equivalence from the ∞-category of simplicial [stable ∞-categories](c:stable-infinity-category) to the ∞-category of connective chain complexes of stable ∞-categories. Its inverse is a categorified Dold-Kan nerve.

hypotheses.text: The objects are [stable ∞-categories](c:stable-infinity-category), and the morphisms are exact functors.
The first side consists of [simplicial objects](c:simplicial-object) in stable ∞-categories.
The second side consists of connective [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) of stable ∞-categories.

conclusion: The categorified normalized chains functor $C$ is an equivalence of ∞-categories, with inverse the categorified nerve $N$.

proofs.name: Categorified normalized chains and nerve
proofs.slogan: Categorify the classical correspondence by defining chains and a nerve for stable ∞-categories, then show that they invert each other.
proofs.scope: An outline of the cited proof. The (∞,2)-categorical definitions and the comparison of the two composites rest on Dyckerhoff's paper.

roles.why: Stable ∞-categories with exact functors replace abelian groups with homomorphisms.
Simplicial stable ∞-categories are the domain of the normalized chains functor.
Chain complexes of stable ∞-categories are the target of $C$ and the domain of the nerve.

steps.slogan: Take the classical Dold-Kan correspondence as the model to categorify.
steps.detail: Classically, normalized chains identify simplicial abelian groups with connective chain complexes. Dyckerhoff replaces abelian groups by [stable ∞-categories](c:stable-infinity-category) and group homomorphisms by exact functors.

steps.slogan: Define the categorified normalized chains functor $C$ on simplicial stable ∞-categories.
steps.detail: In a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of stable ∞-categories the differentials are exact functors, and consecutive composites vanish up to specified coherent data. The paper builds $C$ from a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) and shows that its value is such a complex.

steps.slogan: Define the categorified Dold-Kan nerve $N$ as the candidate inverse of $C$.
steps.detail: For a chain complex $\mathcal B_\bullet$ the paper builds a simplicial stable ∞-category $N(\mathcal B_\bullet)$. For a complex with one term $\mathcal B$ in degree 1, $N$ gives an ∞-categorical version of Waldhausen's $S_\bullet$-construction, which is a [2-Segal space](c:2-segal-space).

steps.slogan: Show that $C$ and $N$ are mutually inverse equivalences of ∞-categories.
steps.detail: The paper compares the composites $CN$ and $NC$ with the identity functors and checks that the comparison maps are equivalences. This is the main technical work of the cited paper, and this outline does not reproduce it.

concepts.c:stable-infinity-category: Stable ∞-categories replace abelian groups as the objects that the correspondence relates.
concepts.c:simplicial-object: The normalized chains functor starts from simplicial objects.
concepts.c:chain-complex: Connective chain complexes of stable ∞-categories are the other side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:2-segal-space: The nerve of a one-term complex is a Waldhausen construction, which is 2-Segal.

source.ref: T. Dyckerhoff, A categorified Dold-Kan correspondence, Selecta Mathematica (New Series) 27 (2021), no. 2, Paper No. 14
source.note: The outline follows the statement and construction of the paper: normalized chains C, nerve N, and the Waldhausen S-construction as the nerve of a one-term complex.

statement: In a plane that satisfies [Hilbert's axioms](c:hilbert-s-axioms) of incidence and order, let $A, B, C$ be non-collinear and let $D$ lie in the interior of the [angle](c:angle) $BAC$. Then ray $AD$ meets the [line segment](c:line-segment) $BC$ at a point between $B$ and $C$.

hypotheses.text: The points $A, B, C$ are not collinear.
The point $D$ lies in the interior of the [angle](c:angle) $BAC$: it is on the same side of line $AB$ as $C$ and on the same side of line $AC$ as $B$.

conclusion: Some point $H$ with $H$ between $B$ and $C$ lies on ray $AD$.

proofs.name: From Pasch's theorem
proofs.slogan: Extend $CA$ beyond $A$, apply Pasch's theorem to the line $AD$ and the triangle $EBC$, and exclude the side $EB$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in the language of [Hilbert's axioms](c:hilbert-s-axioms): sides of a line and betweenness only, with no measure of angles.

roles.why: It makes $B$ lie off line $AC$, so sides of line $AC$ exist and $EBC$ is a triangle.
It places $D$ on the same side of each line as the opposite vertex, which fixes where ray $AD$ lies.

steps.slogan: Extend $CA$ beyond $A$ to a point $E$ with $A$ between $E$ and $C$.
steps.detail: The order axioms give a point $E$ on line $AC$ with $A$ [between](c:betweenness) $E$ and $C$. Then $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AB$, because segment $EC$ meets line $AB$ at $A$.

steps.slogan: Apply Pasch's theorem to triangle $EBC$ and the line $AD$.
steps.detail: The line $\ell = AD$ meets side $EC$ at its inner point $A$. It passes through none of $E$, $B$, $C$, because $D$ lies on neither line $AB$ nor line $AC$. So $\ell$ meets segment $EB$ or segment $BC$.

steps.slogan: Rule out a meeting point of line $AD$ with segment $EB$.
steps.detail: Suppose $G \in \ell$ lies between $E$ and $B$. Then $G$ is on $B$'s side of line $AC$, which is $D$'s side, so $G$ is on ray $AD$ and on $C$'s side of line $AB$. But $G$ is on $E$'s side of line $AB$, which is opposite to $C$'s side. This contradiction rules out $G$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that line $AD$ meets segment $BC$ strictly between $B$ and $C$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give a point $H$ of $\ell$ on segment $BC$. Since $\ell$ avoids $B$ and $C$, the point $H$ is between $B$ and $C$.

steps.slogan: Show that $H$ lies on ray $AD$ and not on the opposite ray.
steps.detail: The point $H$ lies between $B$ and $C$, so it is on $B$'s side of line $AC$, which is $D$'s side. The points of $\ell$ on that side form ray $AD$, so $H$ lies on ray $AD$.

concepts.c:hilbert-s-axioms: The proof uses only incidence, order and plane separation from these axioms.
concepts.c:angle: The interior of the angle fixes the sides of the lines $AB$ and $AC$ that hold $D$.
concepts.c:line-segment: The conclusion is a statement about where a ray meets a segment.
concepts.c:betweenness: Betweenness defines the extension point $E$ and the sides of the lines.

source.note: The standard derivation of the crossbar theorem from Pasch's axiom, as in textbooks on Hilbert's axioms such as Greenberg, Euclidean and Non-Euclidean Geometries.

statement: Let $\xi$ be a real number that is neither [rational](c:rational-number) nor a [quadratic irrational](c:quadratic-irrational). Then there is a constant $C > 0$ with $|\xi - \alpha| \le C\, H(\alpha)^{-3}$ for infinitely many [algebraic numbers](c:algebraic-number) $\alpha$ of degree at most $2$. Here $H(\alpha)$ is the [height](c:height) of the minimal integer polynomial of $\alpha$.

hypotheses.text: The real number $\xi$ is not [rational](c:rational-number).
The real number $\xi$ is not a [quadratic irrational](c:quadratic-irrational).

conclusion: Infinitely many algebraic numbers $\alpha$ of degree at most $2$ satisfy $|\xi - \alpha| \le C\, H(\alpha)^{-3}$.

proofs.name: Minkowski's theorem on quadratic polynomials
proofs.slogan: Use Minkowski's theorem to find integer quadratics that are small at $\xi$, then read off a root close to $\xi$.
proofs.scope: An outline of the cited proof. The control of the derivative in step 3 is the technical core of the paper and is only described here.

roles.why: It rules out a rational $\xi$, so no nonzero integer polynomial of degree at most $2$ vanishes at $\xi$.
It makes $1, \xi, \xi^2$ independent over $\mathbb Q$, which the derivative bound needs.

steps.slogan: Bound the distance from $\xi$ to a root of a polynomial by its value and derivative.
steps.detail: For $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ of degree at most $2$, the logarithmic derivative $P'/P$ is a sum of terms $1/(\xi - \alpha_i)$. So some root $\alpha$ has $|\xi - \alpha| \le 2|P(\xi)|/|P'(\xi)|$. If $|P(\xi)| \ll H(P)^{-2}$ and $|P'(\xi)| \gg H(P)$, then $|\xi - \alpha| \ll H(P)^{-3}$.

steps.slogan: Find integer polynomials with small value at $\xi$ by Minkowski's theorem.
steps.detail: For $X \ge 1$ the convex body $|x_1| \le X$, $|x_2| \le X$, $|x_0 + x_1 \xi + x_2 \xi^2| \le X^{-2}$ has volume $8$. Minkowski's theorem gives a nonzero integer point, that is a polynomial $P = x_0 + x_1 x + x_2 x^2$ with $H(P) \ll X$ and $0 < |P(\xi)| \le X^{-2}$.

steps.slogan: Keep the derivative of the chosen polynomials at $\xi$ of size $H(P)$.
steps.detail: The cited paper bounds $|P'(\xi)|$ from below for suitably chosen polynomials of this kind. The proof uses that $1, \xi, \xi^2$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, and it is the technical core of the paper.

steps.slogan: Pass from the polynomial to a root and count infinitely many distinct roots.
steps.detail: A root $\alpha$ of $P$ satisfies $|\xi - \alpha| \ll H(P)^{-3}$ and $H(\alpha) \ll H(P)$ by Gelfond's inequality, so $|\xi - \alpha| \le C H(\alpha)^{-3}$. Since $P(\xi) \ne 0$ and $|P(\xi)| \le X^{-2}$, new polynomials and roots appear as $X \to \infty$, so infinitely many distinct $\alpha$ occur.

concepts.c:rational-number: Rational numbers are excluded, so no linear polynomial vanishes at $\xi$.
concepts.c:quadratic-irrational: Quadratic irrationals are excluded, so no quadratic polynomial vanishes at $\xi$.
concepts.c:algebraic-number: The approximants are algebraic numbers of degree at most $2$.
concepts.c:height: The height of the approximant measures the size of its minimal polynomial.

source.ref: H. Davenport and W. M. Schmidt, Approximation to real numbers by quadratic irrationals, Acta Arithmetica 13 (1967), 169-176
source.note: The outline gives the shape of the argument: a Minkowski (Dirichlet-type) polynomial of degree 2, a lower bound for its derivative, and a root close to the number.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral), and let $m$ be the distance between the [midpoints](c:midpoint) of its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Then $AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + DA^2 = AC^2 + BD^2 + 4m^2$.

hypotheses.text: The points $A, B, C, D$ are the vertices of a convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral).

proofs.name: Vector expansion
proofs.slogan: Write the vertices as vectors and expand both sides into squared lengths and dot products.
proofs.scope: The identity holds for any four points of a Euclidean space, convex or not. For a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram) the two midpoints coincide, so $m = 0$ and the identity is the parallelogram law.

roles.why: It supplies the four vertices and two diagonals; the proof does not use convexity.

steps.slogan: Name the vertices by position vectors and write the midpoints as half sums.
steps.detail: Let $a, b, c, d$ be the position [vectors](c:vector) of $A, B, C, D$, and put $\Sigma = |a|^2 + |b|^2 + |c|^2 + |d|^2$. The midpoints are $\tfrac12(a+c)$ and $\tfrac12(b+d)$, so $4m^2 = |a + c - b - d|^2$.

steps.slogan: Expand the sum of the four squared sides.
steps.detail: $|a-b|^2 + |b-c|^2 + |c-d|^2 + |d-a|^2 = 2\Sigma - 2(a\cdot b + b\cdot c + c\cdot d + d\cdot a) = 2\Sigma - 2(a+c)\cdot(b+d)$.

steps.slogan: Expand the squared diagonals and the squared midpoint distance.
steps.detail: $|a-c|^2 + |b-d|^2 = \Sigma - 2a\cdot c - 2b\cdot d$, and $|a+c-b-d|^2 = \Sigma + 2a\cdot c + 2b\cdot d - 2(a+c)\cdot(b+d)$.

steps.slogan: Add the two diagonal expansions and compare the total with the side expansion.
steps.detail: The sum of the two expansions of step 3 is $2\Sigma - 2(a+c)\cdot(b+d)$, which equals the result of step 2. Hence $AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + DA^2 = AC^2 + BD^2 + 4m^2$.

concepts.c:quadrilateral: The four vertices of the quadrilateral are the data of the identity.
concepts.c:midpoint: The distance $m$ between the diagonal midpoints is the correction term.
concepts.c:parallelogram: For a parallelogram the midpoints coincide and the identity becomes the parallelogram law.
concepts.c:vector: Position vectors turn squared lengths into dot products.

source.note: The standard vector computation for Euler's quadrilateral theorem.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite abelian group](c:finite-abelian-group) and let $G = A_1 A_2 \cdots A_k$ be a factorization into simplexes $A_i = \{e, g_i, \dots, g_i^{s_i - 1}\}$: every element of $G$ is a product $a_1 \cdots a_k$ with $a_i \in A_i$ in exactly one way. Then some $A_i$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup).

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite abelian group](c:finite-abelian-group).
Each factor has the form $A_i = \{e, g_i, \dots, g_i^{s_i - 1}\}$ with $s_i \ge 1$.
Every element of $G$ is a product $a_1 \cdots a_k$ with $a_i \in A_i$ in exactly one way.

conclusion: For some $i$ the set $A_i$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$, that is $g_i^{s_i} = e$.

proofs.name: Group ring argument
proofs.slogan: Write the factorization as an identity in the group ring and show that a factorization without a subgroup factor is impossible.
proofs.scope: An outline of the cited proof. Steps 1 to 3 set up the argument; the closing computation is that of the cited paper and is not reproduced here.

roles.why: Commutativity makes the group ring commutative and lets the factors be rearranged.
Each factor is a segment of a cycle, so a coset of $\langle g_i \rangle$ is cut into arcs.
Unique factorization gives the identity $A_1 \cdots A_k = G$ in the group ring.

steps.slogan: Write the factorization as a product identity in the group ring $\mathbb Z[G]$.
steps.detail: Write $A_i$ also for the sum of its elements in the [group ring](c:group-ring). Unique factorization says that $A_1 A_2 \cdots A_k = \sum_{g \in G} g$. Hajós used group rings as the main tool of his proof.

steps.slogan: Restate the goal as $g_i^{s_i} = e$ for some factor.
steps.detail: Unique factorization makes $e, g_i, \dots, g_i^{s_i - 1}$ distinct, so $s_i \le \operatorname{ord}(g_i)$. The simplex $A_i$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) if and only if $s_i = \operatorname{ord}(g_i)$, that is $g_i^{s_i} = e$. A factor with $s_i = 1$ is the trivial subgroup, so assume every $s_i \ge 2$.

steps.slogan: Cut each coset of $\langle g_1 \rangle$ into arcs to show that the other factors form a periodic set.
steps.detail: Let $s_1 < n = \operatorname{ord}(g_1)$ and $B = A_2 \cdots A_k$, so $G = A_1 B$ is a direct product. Each coset of $\langle g_1 \rangle$ is a cycle of length $n$, cut into disjoint arcs of length $s_1$ that start at the points of $B$. So these points are equally spaced, and $B g_1^{s_1} = B$ with $g_1^{s_1} \ne e$.

steps.slogan: Finish with the cited argument: a factorization without a subgroup factor cannot exist.
steps.detail: The cited paper completes the proof from the identity of step 1 and the periodicity of step 3, by a computation in the group ring. Hence some factor satisfies $g_i^{s_i} = e$.

concepts.c:finite-abelian-group: The proof uses commutativity and finiteness of $G$ in the group ring.
concepts.c:subgroup: The goal is that some simplex is a subgroup.
concepts.c:group-ring: The factorization becomes a product identity in the group ring of $G$.

source.ref: G. Hajós, Über einfache und mehrfache Bedeckung des n-dimensionalen Raumes mit einem Würfelgitter, Mathematische Zeitschrift 47 (1942), 427-467
source.note: Shorter proofs: T. Szele, Kurzer Beweis des gruppentheoretischen Satzes von Hajós, Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici 24 (1950); see also Stein and Szabó, Algebra and Tiling, Carus Mathematical Monographs 25 (MAA, 1994).

statement: There are absolute constants $c > 0$ and $L$ such that for coprime integers $1 \le a < d$ the least prime $p(a,d)$ in the [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression) $a + nd$, $n \ge 1$, satisfies $p(a,d) < c\, d^{L}$.

hypotheses.text: The integers $a$ and $d$ are [coprime](c:coprime-integers) and satisfy $1 \le a \le d - 1$.

conclusion: The progression $a + nd$ with $n \ge 1$ contains a prime below $c\, d^{L}$.

proofs.name: Log-free zero density and Deuring-Heilbronn
proofs.slogan: Detect primes with Dirichlet characters, bound the zeros near the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, and repel an exceptional zero.
proofs.scope: An outline of Linnik's proof; the value of $L$ is not tracked. Later work gives admissible values such as $L = 5$.

roles.why: Coprimality lets characters modulo $d$ pick out the class of $a$ and makes primes possible.

steps.slogan: Detect the progression with Dirichlet characters modulo $d$.
steps.detail: By orthogonality of [Dirichlet characters](c:dirichlet-character), the sum $\psi(x; d, a)$ of $\Lambda(n)$ over $n \le x$ with $n \equiv a \pmod d$ equals $\varphi(d)^{-1} \sum_\chi \bar\chi(a)\, \psi(x, \chi)$. It suffices to show $\psi(x; d, a) > 0$ for some $x \le d^{L}$.

steps.slogan: Write each $\psi(x, \chi)$ by the explicit formula over the zeros of $L(s, \chi)$.
steps.detail: For each [L-function](c:l-function) $L(s, \chi)$, the explicit formula gives $\psi(x, \chi) = \delta_\chi x - \sum_\rho x^\rho / \rho + {}$ small terms, where $\rho$ runs over the nontrivial zeros. The principal character gives the main term $x$.

steps.slogan: Bound the zeros near the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$ by Linnik's log-free density estimate.
steps.detail: Linnik proved that the number of zeros $\rho$ of all $L(s, \chi)$ modulo $d$ with $\operatorname{Re} \rho \ge \sigma$ and $|\operatorname{Im} \rho| \le T$ is at most $C (dT)^{c(1 - \sigma)}$, with no logarithmic factor. With a [zero-free region](c:zero-free-region), this shows that the zeros add little to $\psi(x, \chi)$ for $x \ge d^{L}$.

steps.slogan: Handle a possible exceptional real zero by the Deuring-Heilbronn phenomenon.
steps.detail: At most one real character modulo $d$ can have a real zero $\beta$ very close to $1$. The Deuring-Heilbronn phenomenon, proved in the second of Linnik's papers, says that such a zero pushes all other zeros farther from $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$. This makes the exceptional term smaller than the main term.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\psi(x; d, a) > 0$ at $x = d^{L}$ and read off a prime.
steps.detail: For $x \ge d^{L}$ the main term $x / \varphi(d)$ exceeds the contribution of the zeros and of the exceptional zero. So $\psi(x; d, a) > 0$. Prime powers with exponent at least $2$ are too few to carry the sum, so a prime $p \equiv a \pmod d$ lies below $x$.

concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: The theorem bounds the first prime of an arithmetic progression.
concepts.c:coprime-integers: Coprimality of $a$ and $d$ is what allows primes in the progression.
concepts.c:dirichlet-character: Characters modulo $d$ separate the residue classes and carry the analysis.
concepts.c:l-function: The zeros of the $L$-functions of the characters control the prime count.
concepts.c:zero-free-region: A zero-free region keeps most zeros away from the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$.

source.ref: U. V. Linnik, On the least prime in an arithmetic progression. I. The basic theorem, Rec. Math. (Mat. Sbornik) N.S. 15(57) (1944), 139-178; II. The Deuring-Heilbronn phenomenon, ibid. 15(57) (1944), 347-368
source.note: The outline follows Linnik's two papers: the density estimate of part I and the zero repulsion of part II.

statement: Let $D$ be a quiver and $T$ a representation of $D$ in finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field $k$. There is a universal $k$-linear [abelian category](c:abelian-category) $\mathcal C(D,T)$ with a [faithful](c:faithful) [exact functor](c:exact-functor) $\omega$ to vector spaces and a lift of $T$ through $\omega$. It is the category of finite-dimensional [comodules](c:comodule) over a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra).

hypotheses.text: The ground ring $k$ is a field.
The object $D$ is a quiver, that is a [directed graph](c:directed-graph), and $T$ gives each vertex a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and each edge a linear map.

conclusion: A universal pair $(\mathcal C(D,T), \omega)$ with a lift $\tilde T$ of $T$ exists, and $\mathcal C(D,T)$ is equivalent to finite-dimensional comodules over the coalgebra $\varinjlim_F \operatorname{End}(T|_F)^\vee$.

proofs.name: Diagram category as a colimit of module categories
proofs.slogan: Build modules over endomorphism algebras of finite subquivers, take their colimit, and test the universal property on a fibre functor.
proofs.scope: An outline of the construction of Nori's diagram category, as in the cited book. The proofs that the colimit is a comodule category and that the lifts are unique are not reproduced here.

roles.why: A field makes endomorphism algebras and their modules $k$-linear and the dual of a finite-dimensional algebra a coalgebra.
Finite subquivers give finite-dimensional algebras $A_F$, and the representation $T$ gives the lifts.

steps.slogan: Treat a finite subquiver $F$ by modules over $A_F = \operatorname{End}(T|_F)$.
steps.detail: An element of $A_F$ is a family of endomorphisms of the spaces $T(v)$, $v \in F$, that commute with all maps $T(e)$. The category $\mathcal C(F)$ of finite-dimensional $A_F$-modules is an [abelian category](c:abelian-category), its forgetful functor to vector spaces is [faithful](c:faithful) and exact, and $T|_F$ lifts to it.

steps.slogan: Pass from finite subquivers to $D$ by a colimit of categories.
steps.detail: For $F \subseteq F'$, restriction along $A_{F'} \to A_F$ gives exact faithful functors $\mathcal C(F) \to \mathcal C(F')$ that respect the forgetful functors. Define $\mathcal C(D,T)$ as the 2-colimit; it carries $\omega$ and the lift of $T$.

steps.slogan: Identify the colimit with comodules over a coalgebra to see that it is abelian.
steps.detail: The cited book identifies $\mathcal C(D,T)$ with finite-dimensional [comodules](c:comodule) over the [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) $\varinjlim_F A_F^\vee$. Such a comodule category is abelian, and its forgetful functor $\omega$ is [exact](c:exact-functor) and faithful.

steps.slogan: Prove the universal property through the endomorphism algebra of a fibre functor.
steps.detail: Let $\omega_B$ be a faithful exact functor from an abelian category $\mathcal B$, with a lift $S$ of $T$. For finite $F$, the objects generated by the $S(v)$ form a category equivalent to modules over $E = \operatorname{End}(\omega_B|)$, by Tannakian reconstruction. The action of $E$ on each $T(v)$ gives an algebra map $E \to A_F$, and restriction along it gives the required functors, compatible in $F$.

concepts.c:directed-graph: The diagram $D$ is a directed graph whose finite subgraphs are exhausted one by one.
concepts.c:abelian-category: The theorem produces an abelian category from a diagram of vector spaces.
concepts.c:faithful: Faithfulness of the fibre functor is what the universal property fixes.
concepts.c:exact-functor: The fibre functor $\omega$ is required to be exact.
concepts.c:comodule: The diagram category is a category of comodules.
concepts.c:coalgebra: The coalgebra is the colimit of the duals of the algebras $A_F$.

source.ref: A. Huber and S. Müller-Stach, Periods and Nori Motives, Ergebnisse der Mathematik und ihrer Grenzgebiete 65, Springer, 2017, chapter 7 (Nori's diagram category)
source.note: The outline follows the construction and the comodule description of the diagram category in the book.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a nondegenerate [parallelogram](c:parallelogram). Erect a [square](c:square) outward on each of its four sides. Then the centers of the four squares are the vertices of a square.

hypotheses.text: The quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a nondegenerate [parallelogram](c:parallelogram).
A [square](c:square) is erected outward on each side of $ABCD$.

conclusion: The four centers of the erected squares are the vertices of a [square](c:square).

proofs.name: Complex numbers
proofs.slogan: Put the center of the parallelogram at the origin and show that the four centers are one point turned by right angles.
proofs.scope: Thébault's problem I only. The record also names problems II and III, which are other statements and are not proved here.

roles.why: A parallelogram has vertices $a, b, -a, -b$ around its center, which simplifies all four centers.
Outward squares fix the center of each as a half-side turned by a right angle.

steps.slogan: Place the parallelogram in the complex plane with its center at $0$.
steps.detail: Take $A = a$, $B = b$, $C = -a$, $D = -b$ in counterclockwise order, so the common midpoint of the diagonals is $0$. Nondegeneracy means $a / b$ is not real.

steps.slogan: Write the center of the outward square on each side.
steps.detail: Outward is to the right of a side directed counterclockwise, and the right normal is $-i$ times the side. So the center on side $XY$ is $\tfrac12(X + Y) - \tfrac i2 (Y - X)$. This gives $O_1 = \tfrac12(a + b) - \tfrac i2 (b - a)$ on $AB$ and $O_2 = \tfrac12(b - a) + \tfrac i2 (a + b)$ on $BC$.

steps.slogan: Show that opposite centers are symmetric about $0$.
steps.detail: The same formula on $CD$ and $DA$ gives $O_3 = -O_1$ and $O_4 = -O_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $O_2$ is $O_1$ turned by a right angle.
steps.detail: Expanding gives $i\,O_1 = \tfrac i2 (a + b) + \tfrac12 (b - a) = O_2$. So $O_2$ is the [rotation](c:rotation) of $O_1$ by $90^\circ$ about $0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $O_1, iO_1, -O_1, -iO_1$ are the vertices of a square.
steps.detail: These four points are the images of $O_1$ under the rotations by multiples of a right angle about $0$. Also $O_1 \ne 0$: the center of the outward square on $AB$ lies on the side of line $AB$ away from the parallelogram, and $0$ lies on the other side. So they form a [square](c:square) centered at $0$.

concepts.c:parallelogram: Its symmetry about the center makes opposite square centers symmetric too.
concepts.c:square: Squares are both the erected figures and the shape of the conclusion.
concepts.c:rotation: A rotation by $90^\circ$ maps one center to the next.

source.note: The classical complex-number computation for Thébault's problem I (squares erected on a parallelogram).

statement: Let $M$ be a closed connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold). If every [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) in $M$ lies in a topological ball in $M$, then $M$ is homeomorphic to the [3-sphere](c:3-sphere).

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a closed (compact, boundaryless) connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold).
Every [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) in $M$ lies in a subset of $M$ homeomorphic to the closed unit ball.

conclusion: The manifold $M$ is homeomorphic to the [3-sphere](c:3-sphere).

proofs.name: Reduction to the Poincaré conjecture
proofs.slogan: Each loop is homotopic to a curve inside a ball, so the manifold is simply connected and Perelman's theorem gives the 3-sphere.
proofs.scope: The manifold is closed: a compact ball has boundary and meets the curve condition, but it is not the 3-sphere. The converse is immediate, since a compact set that misses a point of $S^3$ lies in a ball of $S^3 \setminus \{pt\} \cong \mathbb R^3$, and Bing's own proof of 1958 avoids the Poincaré conjecture.

roles.why: Closedness and connectedness are what the Poincaré conjecture needs, and triangulation lets loops be made polygonal.
A ball is contractible, so every simple closed curve inside one is null-homotopic.

steps.slogan: Replace each loop in $M$ by a homotopic simple closed curve.
steps.detail: By Moise's theorem $M$ is triangulable, so every loop is homotopic to a polygonal loop. Two curves in a 3-manifold miss each other in general position, so a generic polygonal loop has no self-intersection. Hence every loop is homotopic to a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve).

steps.slogan: Contract the simple closed curve inside the ball that contains it.
steps.detail: By hypothesis the curve lies in a topological ball, which is contractible. So the curve is null-homotopic in the ball, and hence in $M$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $M$ is a simply connected manifold.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 show that every loop in $M$ is null-homotopic, and $M$ is connected. So $\pi_1(M)$ is trivial and $M$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).

steps.slogan: Apply the Poincaré conjecture to the closed simply connected 3-manifold.
steps.detail: Perelman's theorem states that a closed simply connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) is homeomorphic to the [3-sphere](c:3-sphere). So $M \cong S^3$.

concepts.c:3-manifold: The Poincaré conjecture is a statement about closed 3-manifolds.
concepts.c:3-sphere: The 3-sphere is the manifold that the proof must identify.
concepts.c:simple-closed-curve: The hypothesis is about simple closed curves, to which every loop is reduced.
concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity is the property that the curve hypothesis gives.

source.note: A short reduction to the Poincaré conjecture (Perelman). The original proof is R. H. Bing, Necessary and sufficient conditions that a 3-manifold be S^3, Annals of Mathematics 68 (1958), 17-37, which does not use it.

statement: Let $K \subset \mathbb R^n$, $n \ge 2$, be an origin-symmetric [convex body](c:convex-body). For $x \ne 0$ put $\|x\| = |x| / \operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(K \cap x^\perp)$ and $\|0\| = 0$. Then $\|\cdot\|$ is a [norm](c:norm).

hypotheses.text: The set $K$ is an origin-symmetric [convex body](c:convex-body) in $\mathbb R^n$, so $0$ is an interior point of $K$.
The dimension satisfies $n \ge 2$.

conclusion: The function $\|\cdot\|$ is a [norm](c:norm); equivalently the star body with radial function $u \mapsto \operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(K \cap u^\perp)$ is convex.

proofs.name: Brunn concavity of parallel sections
proofs.slogan: Slice the body by parallel planes, use the concavity of section volumes, and reduce convexity of the unit ball to a planar inequality.
proofs.scope: An outline of Busemann's proof for $n \ge 3$. The case $n = 2$ is direct: sections are chords, so the unit ball is $K$ turned by a right angle and scaled by $2$.

roles.why: Convexity gives Brunn concavity of sections, symmetry gives evenness, and an interior origin gives positive volumes.
It makes hyperplane sections of positive dimension and gives a complement $E$ on which Brunn's theorem applies.

steps.slogan: Reduce convexity of the unit ball to a two-dimensional plane through the origin.
steps.detail: A positive homogeneous function is a [norm](c:norm) once its unit ball is convex, and convexity of a star body is tested on $2$-planes $P$ through $0$. Fix such a plane $P$ and put $E = P^\perp$, of dimension $n - 2$.

steps.slogan: Slice $K$ by the planes parallel to $E$ to get a profile function on $P$.
steps.detail: Put $\varphi(z) = \operatorname{vol}_{n-2}(K \cap (z + E))$ for $z \in P$. For a unit vector $u \in P$, Fubini gives $\operatorname{vol}_{n-1}(K \cap u^\perp) = \int_{\mathbb R} \varphi(t\, Ju)\, dt$, where $J$ is the right-angle rotation of $P$.

steps.slogan: Show that the profile is even and that a power of it is concave.
steps.detail: The function $\varphi$ is even because $K = -K$. By the Brunn-Minkowski theorem, $\varphi^{1/(n-2)}$ is concave on its support, which is the projection of the [convex body](c:convex-body) $K$ to $P$.

steps.slogan: Prove the planar inequality for such profiles.
steps.detail: For $x \in P \setminus \{0\}$ put $\rho(x) = \int_0^\infty \varphi(tx)\, dt$. The cited paper proves that $1/\rho$ is convex when $\varphi$ is even and a power of a concave function on its support. This is its central estimate.

steps.slogan: Read off convexity of the unit ball and the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: On $P$ one has $\|x\| = 1 / (2\rho(Jx))$, so $\|\cdot\|$ is convex on every plane $P$. Hence the unit ball is convex and $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm. It is finite and positive because $0$ is interior to $K$.

concepts.c:convex-body: Convexity of $K$ gives concave section volumes, and symmetry gives evenness.
concepts.c:norm: The goal is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|$, which follows from a convex unit ball.

source.ref: H. Busemann, A theorem on convex bodies of the Brunn-Minkowski type, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA 35 (1949), 27-31
source.note: The outline reduces to planes through the origin by Fubini and Brunn's concavity theorem; the planar estimate is the core of the paper.

statement: The number of [sum-free sets](c:sum-free-set) $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$, that is of sets with no $x, y, z \in A$ satisfying $x + y = z$, is $O(2^{N/2})$.

hypotheses.text: The number $N$ is a positive integer, and the sets are subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$.

conclusion: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that $\{1, \dots, N\}$ has at most $C\, 2^{N/2}$ sum-free subsets for every $N$.

new_concepts.name: container method
new_concepts.reminder: Cover all objects of a kind by a small family of sets, each of which holds few such objects.
new_concepts.definition: A container family for a class of subsets of a ground set is a family of subsets such that every member of the class lies in one of them. Counting the class then reduces to counting inside each container.

proofs.name: Fourier containers
proofs.slogan: Cover all sum-free sets by few containers built with Fourier analysis, then count the sum-free subsets inside each container.
proofs.scope: An outline of Green's proof; Sapozhenko proved the theorem independently by graph-theoretic methods. The bound is sharp, because the $2^{\lceil N/2 \rceil}$ subsets of the odd numbers are all sum-free.

roles.why: It fixes the ground set $\{1, \dots, N\}$ on which the containers and the counts live.

steps.slogan: Reduce the count to counting inside a family of containers.
steps.detail: The cited paper builds a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$, the [containers](c:container-method), such that every [sum-free set](c:sum-free-set) lies in some container. The number of sum-free sets is then at most the sum, over $C \in \mathcal F$, of the number of sum-free subsets of $C$.

steps.slogan: Build the containers from the Fourier transform of a sum-free set.
steps.detail: A sum-free set $A$ has no solutions of $x + y = z$, and the number of such solutions is a sum of products of three Fourier coefficients of $A$. For dense $A$ this forces a large coefficient at a nonzero frequency. The paper turns this structure into the containers.

steps.slogan: Count the sum-free subsets inside each container.
steps.detail: A container $C$ has at most $2^{|C|}$ subsets, and the paper bounds the number of sum-free subsets of the larger containers more strongly. This counting is the second main part of the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Add the counts over all containers to get $O(2^{N/2})$.
steps.detail: The paper shows that the family $\mathcal F$ is small and that each container holds few sum-free sets. Summing over the containers gives at most $C\, 2^{N/2}$ sum-free subsets.

concepts.c:sum-free-set: Sum-free sets are the objects counted and covered by the containers.
concepts.c:container-method: Containers reduce counting sum-free sets to counting inside a few sets.

source.ref: B. Green, The Cameron-Erdős conjecture, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 36 (2004), 769-778
source.note: The outline follows Green's proof, which builds a family of containers by Fourier analysis; Sapozhenko's independent proof is combinatorial.
